name: Surgical Robotics and AI
blurb: New robotic surgery systems and the AI in them.
title: Surgical Robotics and AI
answer: Robotic surgery is opening up beyond one dominant platform: Medtronic's Hugo and CMR Surgical's Versius Plus both received FDA clearance in December 2025. AI features in surgery so far mostly assist, such as video analysis and guidance, rather than acting autonomously.

reading.body:
Two new surgical robot platforms cleared the FDA in December 2025, and the AI in them assists rather than operates.

Medtronic's Hugo and CMR Surgical's Versius Plus both received clearance that month, ending a market long defined by a single dominant platform. The AI features shipping today are narrow and supportive: video analysis, guidance overlays, instrument tracking, and performance measurement for training. Autonomous surgical action remains research, with a surgeon in control of every cleared system.

The competitive effect is on cost, and the durable asset is data. Every procedure a robot performs generates motion and video records that can train later assistance features and build evidence on outcomes. That makes installed base and procedure volume the things to watch, not the feature list on a clearance letter.

What this does not cover is scale. The data names two clearances and no installed base, procedure counts, or price figures, so it cannot show how much share is actually shifting or how quickly. It also gives no timeline for when autonomous features might clear, and the cited research on surgical robotics is thin and recent, so treat the assistive-only characterization as current rather than permanent.

explainer:
Robotic assisted surgery uses a console controlled by the surgeon to move instruments through small incisions with greater precision and visibility. For years one system dominated the market, but new entrants are now cleared in the United States, widening choice and putting pressure on cost.

AI in surgery today mostly assists rather than acts. Uses include analysing surgical video to identify phases and anatomy, providing guidance overlays, tracking instruments, measuring performance for training, and documenting procedures. Autonomous surgical actions remain experimental. The longer term asset is data: robotic systems capture detailed records of motion and video from every procedure, which can train future assistance features and support evidence on outcomes.

What AI does in surgical robotics today

Surgical robots in use today are controlled by surgeons; they do not operate on their own. AI appears around that control: stabilising images, identifying anatomy and instruments in the video feed, warning when a tool approaches a structure that should not be cut, tracking the stages of a procedure, and after the operation, analysing the video to assess technique. Autonomous steps exist in research and in narrow tasks such as suturing in laboratory settings, but a robot that performs an operation unaided is not an approved product.

Why regulators are careful

A surgical device failure can cause immediate harm, so these systems sit in the highest device risk classes. Adding AI raises questions regulators have not fully settled: how to validate a model that sees a different anatomy in every patient, how to handle updates to the model after approval, and how to divide responsibility between the surgeon, the hospital and the manufacturer when an AI warning is wrong or missed. Approvals so far have been for specific, bounded functions with the surgeon in control.

What is likely next

The near term direction is more assistance, not autonomy: better recognition of anatomy, real time guidance drawn from thousands of recorded procedures, skills assessment for training surgeons, and planning tools that use patient imaging. Each is a separate regulatory question. The data these robots generate, hours of annotated video per procedure, is also becoming an asset in its own right, which raises consent and ownership questions hospitals and manufacturers are only starting to negotiate.
